items.title: Jurists accuse Bukele's government of crimes against humanity

featured_image.name: El Salvador likely committed crimes against humanity during state of  emergency, jurists say | Reuters

items.description:
A group of international legal experts filed a formal complaint with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights on Tuesday, accusing El Salvador's government of committing crimes against humanity during its four-year state of emergency. The 275-page report represents the most serious accusation of human rights violations leveled against President Nayib Bukele's administration since he took office in 2019.[1][2]

The complaint, filed by the International Group of Experts for the Investigation of Human Rights Violations under the State of Exception in El Salvador — known by its Spanish acronym GIPES — alleges there are "reasonable grounds" to conclude that crimes against humanity, as defined by Article 7 of the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, are taking place in the Central American nation. The report contends that the violations stem from a state policy "known and even promoted by the highest levels of President Nayib Bukele's government."[3][4][1]

items.title: Merz calls Israel's West Bank settlement push a 'big mistake'

featured_image.name: Germany's Merz says Israel's West Bank settlement plan a ...

items.description:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Tuesday sharply criticized Israel's settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank, describing the moves as "annexation steps" and calling on the Israeli government to reverse course. Speaking at a joint press conference with Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš in Berlin, Merz warned that advancing the so-called E1 settlement project would "further complicate the two-state solution."[1][2]

"I want to be clear here," Merz said. "The annexation steps discussed in Jerusalem will further complicate the two-state solution." He added that the German government "urgently demands the abandonment of such steps" regarding the E1 area, calling the project "a big mistake."[3][1]

items.title: Iran launches drone strikes on Haifa refinery in second attack in three days

featured_image.name: Iranian missile attacks damage Haifa oil refinery and ...

items.description:
Iran's military announced Tuesday that it launched drone strikes against Israel's oil and gas refinery and fuel storage facilities in the northern port city of Haifa, marking the second Iranian attack on the facility in three days and a deepening of the energy infrastructure war between the two countries.

"Iran's Army Air Force launched suicide drones targeting oil, gas, and fuel storage facilities of the Israeli regime in Haifa in response to attacks on Iran's oil depots," the spokesman for the Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, the unified command of Iran's armed forces, said in a statement carried by Iranian state media. The Haifa refinery, operated by the Bazan Group, is Israel's largest oil-processing facility, with a capacity of 197,000 barrels per day. It had reportedly shut down several units last week as a precautionary measure.[1][2]

items.title: Trump administration asks Israel to halt strikes on Iran's oil infrastructure

featured_image.name: Scoop: U.S. dismayed by Israel's Iran fuel strikes, sources say - Axios

items.description:
The Trump administration on Monday asked Israel to stop conducting strikes on Iranian energy facilities, marking the first time Washington has sought to restrain its ally since the two nations launched their joint military campaign against Iran on February 28, according to Axios.[1]

The request came after Israeli warplanes struck at least 30 fuel storage facilities in and around Tehran on Saturday night, igniting massive fires that blanketed the Iranian capital in toxic black smoke and triggered warnings of acid rain for the city's 10 million residents. The strikes represented the first Israeli attacks on Iran's energy infrastructure since the war began.[2][3][4][5]

items.title: Half of Iran's missiles carry cluster warheads, IDF says

featured_image.name: Israel says Iran is using cluster munitions. What to know ...

items.description:
Roughly half of the approximately 300 ballistic missiles Iran has launched at Israel since the war began on February 28 have carried cluster bomb warheads, the Israel Defense Forces disclosed on Tuesday, as the deadly munitions claimed two more lives in central Israel.[1][2]

The cluster warheads explode at high altitude, dispersing dozens of smaller bomblets — each containing several kilograms of explosives — over a radius of about 10 kilometers, according to the IDF Home Front Command. The weapons pose a particular challenge because the scattered submunitions are difficult for air defense systems to intercept once they separate from the main missile body.[3][2]

items.title: IRGC says Iran will decide when war ends, threatens Gulf oil blockade

featured_image.name: Trump gives mixed messages about when the war with Iran will ...

items.description: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps on Tuesday dismissed President Donald Trump's assertions that the US-led war against Iran was nearing its end, declaring that Tehran — not Washington — would determine when the conflict concludes. The sharp rebuke came alongside a threat to halt all oil exports from the Persian Gulf, raising the specter of a prolonged disruption to global energy markets.

items.title: US Navy refuses escort requests through Hormuz

featured_image.name: US signals readiness to escort tankers through Hormuz as traffic thins but  no mission launched

items.description: The US Navy has refused near-daily requests from the shipping industry for military escorts through the Strait of Hormuz since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran on February 28, telling industry leaders the risk of attacks remains too high, according to a Reuters report citing three shipping industry sources familiar with the matter. The refusal stands in sharp contrast to President Donald Trump's repeated assurances that the Navy stands ready to escort tankers through the waterway whenever needed.[1][2]

items.title: Macron to convene G7 leaders call on Iran crisis, energy prices

featured_image.name: Macron to host G7 leaders call on Iran crisis, energy prices ...

items.description:
French President Emmanuel Macron will convene a call with Group of Seven leaders on Wednesday to address the Iran crisis and soaring energy prices, his office announced on Tuesday, as governments scramble to contain the economic fallout from the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.[1][2]

The leaders' call comes after G7 energy ministers met earlier on Tuesday but stopped short of agreeing to release strategic oil reserves, instead asking the International Energy Agency to assess the situation before acting. IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol responded by convening an extraordinary meeting of the agency's member governments to evaluate "current security of supply and market conditions" and determine whether to make emergency stocks available.[3][4][5][1]

items.title: Iran deploys naval mines in Strait of Hormuz, US intelligence says

featured_image.name: Iran begins mining Strait of Hormuz as Washington's tanker ...

items.description:
Iran has begun deploying naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz shipping lanes, according to U.S. intelligence, a dangerous escalation that threatens to deepen the blockade of the world's most critical energy corridor just as Washington's credibility on reopening it suffered a blow on Tuesday.

Small Iranian craft capable of carrying two to three mines each have been detected moving into the waterway, CBS News senior White House reporter Jennifer Jacobs reported on X, citing reporting by Jim LaPorta. While Iran's total mine stockpile is not publicly known, estimates over the years have ranged from roughly 2,000 to 6,000 naval mines of Iranian, Chinese, and Russian-made variants.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Iran begins laying mines in Strait of Hormuz, CNN reports

featured_image.name: G7 energy ministers to meet Tuesday morning to discuss release of oil reserves, sources say

items.description:
Iran has begun laying mines in the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway through which roughly 20% of the world's crude oil passes, according to CNN, citing two people familiar with U.S. intelligence. The move deepens a supply crisis triggered by the U.S.-Israeli military campaign against Iran that began on February 28, leaving an estimated 15 million barrels per day of crude oil production and additional refined fuel stranded in the Persian Gulf.[1]

The mining operation remains limited so far, with only a few dozen mines deployed in recent days, but Iran retains the capacity to lay hundreds more. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has warned that any ship attempting to transit the strait would face attack, effectively rendering the passage closed since the conflict's start.[2][1]

items.title: US destroys 16 Iranian mine-laying vessels near Strait of Hormuz

featured_image.name: US-flagged tanker challenged by Iranian gunboats in Strait of Hormuz

items.description: U.S. Central Command said American forces eliminated 16 Iranian mine-laying vessels near the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, escalating a confrontation over the waterway that carries roughly 20 percent of the world's daily oil supply. The strikes came as Iran's Revolutionary Guards vowed to block all oil exports from the region for as long as the war continues.[1][2]

items.title: Witkoff likely to visit Israel next week to coordinate Iran war plans

featured_image.name: Steve Witkoff visit tests Israel's limits on possible Iran deal

items.description:
White House special envoy Steve Witkoff said Tuesday that he will likely travel to Israel next week alongside Jared Kushner to coordinate military strategy with Israeli leaders as the US-led campaign against Iran enters its second week.

In a CNBC interview on March 10, Witkoff said the United States has "destroyed almost all of their enrichment capability and conversion capability," while acknowledging that Iran's nuclear program has not been entirely eliminated. He added that Iran has shown no interest in returning to negotiations since the US and Israel launched Operation Epic Fury on February 28.[1][2]

items.title: Chevron, Shell near first major Venezuela oil deals since Maduro's capture

featured_image.name: Venezuela approves new law opening its oil industry as Trump ...

items.description:
Chevron and Shell are closing in on the first major oil production agreements with Venezuela since the U.S. military captured President Nicolás Maduro in January, according to a Reuters exclusive citing five sources close to the negotiations.[1][2]

The deals would allow both companies to expand output in some of Venezuela's most coveted oil regions, marking the most concrete steps yet toward what President Donald Trump has described as a $100 billion effort to rebuild the country's battered oil sector after decades of mismanagement under Maduro and his predecessor Hugo Chávez.[2][1]

items.title: Pentagon says US hit 5,000 targets in Iran's first 10 days of war

featured_image.name: Hegseth says Tuesday "most intense day" of U.S. attacks on Iran

items.description:
The United States and Israel unleashed what the Pentagon called their heaviest bombardment of Iran on Tuesday, as Operation Epic Fury entered its 11th day with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth declaring the strikes would mark the "most intense day" since the war began on February 28.

General Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, told reporters at the Pentagon that U.S. forces have struck more than 5,000 targets across Iran in the first 10 days of the campaign, while more than 50 Iranian naval vessels have been damaged or destroyed. Hegseth said the operation's core objectives remain the destruction of Iran's missile stockpiles and launchers, the elimination of its navy, and the permanent denial of nuclear weapons.[1][2][3]

items.title: Israel says it's not seeking 'endless war' as strikes on Tehran intensify

featured_image.name: Israel not seeking endless war with Iran, foreign minister ...

items.description: Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar said on Tuesday that Israel does not want a prolonged conflict with Iran and will consult with the United States on when to halt military operations, declining to offer any timeline for the war's conclusion as strikes on Tehran intensified on the 11th day of fighting.[1][2]

items.title: Iran war fuels calls to accelerate renewable energy shift

featured_image.name: Could War in Iran Spur a Global Energy Crisis?

items.description: The U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, now entering its second week, has thrown global energy markets into turmoil and intensified calls from analysts, climate groups, and world leaders to accelerate the transition to renewable energy — arguing that the crisis exposes the dangers of continued dependence on fossil fuels.

items.title: Hegseth warns of 'most intense' day of strikes on Iran

featured_image.name: Pete Hegseth says Iran's strikes backfired, strengthened US Gulf ties

items.description: The United States and Israel unleashed their most intense wave of airstrikes against Iran on Tuesday, the 11th day of a war that has upended global energy markets and drawn warnings of a widening conflict. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the escalation during a press briefing, declaring that the day would see "the most fighters, bombers, and strikes yet" deployed against Iranian targets.[1]

items.title: US strikes Iran mine-laying vessels as escort claim collapses

featured_image.name: Iran-US tensions: What would blocking Strait of Hormuz mean for oil, LNG?

items.description:
The United States military is actively striking Iranian mine-laying vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff said on Tuesday, as the crisis over the world's most critical energy chokepoint deepened on the same day the US Energy Secretary was forced to delete a false claim about escorting a tanker through the waterway.

"CENTCOM continues today to hunt and strike mine-laying vessels and mine storage facilities," General Dan Caine told reporters on March 10, adding that the US had sunk or destroyed more than 50 Iranian naval ships in the first 10 days of the campaign, according to Reuters. The acknowledgment that Iran has mobilized mine-warfare assets into the strait marks a new and potentially lasting threat to a waterway that carries roughly 20 percent of the world's oil supply.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: New study finds no lab-origin signal for COVID-19 but flags 1977 flu

featured_image.name: Scientists discover key clue in pandemic viruses that reveal if they were made in a lab... including Covid and 'Russian flu'

items.description: A study published last week in the journal Cell offers researchers a new tool for one of the most contentious questions in modern science: how to tell whether a pandemic virus emerged from nature or from a laboratory. The research, led by evolutionary biologist Joel Wertheim at the University of California San Diego School of Medicine, analyzed seven major viral outbreaks from recent decades and found that most pandemic viruses show no signs of being pre-adapted for humans before their outbreaks — with one notable exception.[1][2]

items.title: Iran strikes Gulf desalination, energy sites as war widens

featured_image.name: ‘Reprehensible’: New wave of Iranian missiles, drones target Gulf nations

items.description: A widening war between Iran and a US-Israeli coalition has turned the Middle East's energy infrastructure into a battlefield, with both sides targeting oil facilities, tankers, and shipping routes in an escalation that has effectively shut down the Strait of Hormuz and sent crude prices surging past $115 a barrel.
